I've been working this land for 55 years. I know Quzhou's soil, I know the seasons here, and I know what this wheat-maize rotation needs. My farm is small — 3 mu — and there are only two of us in the household now. I have to be careful about labor because I can't do as much heavy work as I used to. I hire machinery for plowing and harvesting these days. That's just the reality at my age.

**Wheat (winter crop, planted October, harvested June):**
The whole 3 mu goes to wheat over winter. I use the improved variety the local seed station sells — I've used it for years and it performs reliably here. I apply a full base fertilizer at planting: urea and phosphate mixed in. I split my nitrogen — put most down as base, then topdress at the jointing stage. This area is dry, so I irrigate at sowing if soil is too dry, then at tillering, jointing, and heading — four times usually. I'll do two pesticide passes: one herbicide in winter when weeds come up, one fungicide spray in spring when powdery mildew risk gets high. For tillage I use rotary before planting, hired machine comes and does it.

**Maize (summer crop, planted June, harvested October):**
Right after wheat harvest, I turn the field around fast and plant hybrid maize seed — the same hybrid I've been buying from the county seed company for years. The season is short so I use rotary tillage or sometimes no-tillage to get seed in the ground quickly. Maize gets heavy nitrogen — I base-apply some with phosphorus, then topdress at the 6-8 leaf stage which is the critical time. Summer rains help but I still irrigate 3 times: at planting if dry, at tasseling, and at grain fill. Two pesticide applications — one for stem borer, one combined herbicide early on.

I'm not changing anything dramatic this year. At my age, stability matters more than experimenting.
